prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realisation as a many-atom clock with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B013 as the whole prize, to Katori and Ye, and my view is now firmer than in round 1 because the objections have been tested rather than only repeated. The scientific core is a mechanism I can state in one sentence: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift is equal for both clock levels, and thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly and interrogated at once without Stark or motional shifts. That is what separates it from the single-ion clocks honoured in 2012 and from the frequency comb honoured in 2005; an ion clock cannot offer the many-atom statistical gain, and a comb is the readout, not the lattice. The 10^-18 level has been reproduced at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST and through fibre-linked comparisons, which answers the question I always ask about independent confirmation. The two credited roles are distinct, Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clocks, Ye for the accuracy, stability and many-body clock. I note honestly that the convergence on B013 is partly post-reading: several members, and I myself in the sense that B035 was my opening first choice, moved here. I therefore do not rely on the count. I rely on mechanism, reproducibility and clean two-name credit, which are the things I would check for a detector result in my own field.
statement.case_against: The chair's first question remains the hardest one: can the committee state what is new without appearing to award a third clock prize? My answer is a citation tied to the lattice concept and the 10^-18 many-atom realisation, not to clocks, combs or the second in general. Remaining weaknesses are real. No delivered fundamental-physics result (a varying constant, a dark-sector limit) has come out of the clocks yet, so the discovery value is prospective and the achievement is a new measurement capability. The redefinition of the second is still pending. Credit beyond two names (Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Hollberg and the Yb and Al+ lineages) cannot be repaired within the three-person cap, and I am not an atomic physicist, so I cannot independently weigh the early lattice-clock proposals. I would want an expert review of that priority record before the final ballot. I judge these as limits on how the citation should be phrased, not as reasons to choose a candidate with worse attribution or less independent confirmation.

responses.point: Stefan argues that the magic-wavelength idea is a separate concept and the many-atom statistical gain is something ion clocks cannot offer, so the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes does not hold, but the citation must be written carefully around the lattice concept.
responses.response: I agree and I think this is the answer to the chair's novelty question. I would add a test for the citation: it should still be true if the words clock and second were removed from it, so it should name magic-wavelength trapping and the many-atom 10^-18 realisation. That wording makes the distinction from ion control and combs visible to a reader outside the field. Where I am more cautious than Stefan is on credit. He lists Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom and Takamoto as hands-on contributors, and I do not think we can wave that away by calling a Nobel prize a recognition of performance. Two names is defensible only if the early proposal is Katori's and the accuracy programme is Ye's, and that is exactly what I want an outside reviewer to confirm.

responses.point: Eva supports B013 on the mechanism and reproducibility, but notes that no fundamental-physics result has come from the clocks yet, that Lemonde, Hollberg and the JILA and SYRTE teams may have claims, and asks whether pairing the clock with a B001 part would be stronger.
responses.response: On the missing fundamental result I would draw the line this way: the demonstrated capability is already decisive, for instance gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, which is a new quantitative measurement of a known effect and not a promise. A varying-constant or dark-sector limit would be more decisive, and I would not wait for one. On a second part with B001, I considered it seriously. I do not add it, because B001 has no agreed laureate set (Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger versus Zoller, with Cirac on the ballot but on no member's list), and a second part chosen to fill space would weaken a clean single prize. I would revisit it only if the committee settles B001 credit. On Lemonde and Hollberg, I accept that I cannot weigh them from memory either, which is again a reason for expert review.

responses.point: Olle keeps B048 as a new state of matter with a stable twenty-year interpretation, but concedes that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 3D topological insulator work make the three-name set fragile, and names B013 as the safer fallback.
responses.response: I respect the argument that a new state of matter is what the committee has traditionally valued, and I defer to Olle on the physics. But he himself states the fatal problem: Zhang's death means the decisive HgTe proposal cannot be repaired, and the 3D work cannot fit within three names. My own test is whether the credited contribution was decisive and whether the credit survives scrutiny; B048 as written does not pass the second part. I would ask Olle whether a narrower 2D quantum spin Hall prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can be defended as complete without BHZ. If he cannot say yes, I think his own fallback, B013, is the right place to end up, and I would rather he is persuaded on that basis than because of the support count.

responses.point: Bernhard argues that Aharonov-Bohm and the Berry phase are the unifying root of the Chern-number, quantum Hall and band-topology programmes, but admits that Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Simon and Mead-Truhlar priority and Bohm's death make the attribution awkward.
responses.response: The unifying-idea argument is a serious one and I am not dismissing it as an afterthought. My difficulty is the same as his: a prize with the priority questions he lists, and with Bohm deceased, forces the citation to say that the effect was discovered by one living person of a pair. I cannot judge the historical priority in quantum theory, and a prize built on contested priority is the opposite of what I look for, namely a result with a decisive experiment and a clear originator. I would ask Bernhard whether he can write a priority statement that survives Ehrenberg-Siday and Pancharatnam. If not, I would invite him to move to B013, which he already lists as a fallback.

responses.point: Ulf moved from IceCube to B013 but keeps B035 as first alternative, and says he would reopen it if a clean way to credit it were found.
responses.response: I have looked for that clean credit again and have not found it. The diffuse flux is the real discovery, but naming Halzen and Spiering omits the DUMAND and AMANDA lineage and the collaboration leadership, and I will not propose a citation that I think is unfair just because B035 was my opening first choice. I keep B035 as my first alternative and agree with Ulf that it can return in a later year when source catalogues are firmer. I also agree with his own admission that he is trading discovery value for attribution certainty. I accept that trade for B013, but I do not hide that it is a trade, and the citation should be written so that it does not claim more than a new measurement capability.

responses.point: Eva notes that the optical comb is a necessary technical foundation for any optical clock, so the lattice contribution must be shown to be distinct and not a better version of work already honoured.
responses.response: I think Eva's point is correct and it should be conceded in the citation rather than argued around. The comb is the readout that makes optical clocks countable, and that is the 2005 prize. The ion clock is the 2012 prize. What neither of those provide is a neutral-atom ensemble held in a lattice at the magic wavelength, which is Katori's concept, and the demonstration that this reaches 10^-18 with the systematics under control, which is Ye's. If the committee agrees that this is the distinct element, the third-clock-prize charge does not hold. If a majority cannot agree that it is distinct, I would want to hear that before the vote and not after.

uncertainties: Whether an outside expert review of early lattice-clock proposals would add or replace a name beside Katori and Ye, such as Ludlow, Lemke, Lemonde or Takamoto
Whether the committee agrees that magic-wavelength trapping plus many-atom 10^-18 operation is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second or for a delivered fundamental-physics result; I do not think we should, but the committee may differ
Atomic physics is outside my expertise, so my view on priority in the clock lineage is second-hand
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B013, Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) are in astroparticle and gamma-ray work, not atomic clocks, and I rely on colleagues and outside reviewers for priority in the clock lineage. B035, my alternative, is in my own broader field of astroparticle physics, so I would flag possible proximity there, though I know of no personal tie to Halzen or Spiering. As Chair I record that I am in the B013 group, and that I wish the final vote to rest on the scientific case and not on support counts.
